title: How To Handle A Student Who Doesn't Like You https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2023/04/21/how-to-handle-a-student-who-doesnt-like-you/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin addresses the situation of a student who is friendly with classmates and compliant with work, but visibly cold toward the teacher, and warns against the natural instinct to directly ask what's wrong. He explains that such coldness is almost never personal, and more often reflects distrust of adults in general built up from past experiences of neglect or hurt. Approaching the student directly, he argues, only pushes them further away by associating the teacher with the 'fake charmers' who disappointed them before, and it risks the teacher taking the rejection personally and reacting defensively. His recommended approach is to stay focused outward on the whole class, remain consistently and unconditionally pleasant, and let the student approach on their own timetable, trusting that sustained ordinary kindness eventually earns even a distrustful student's respect.
points: A student's coldness toward a teacher is almost never personal — it usually reflects distrust of adults built from past experience.
Directly questioning the student ('Did I do something to upset you?') tends to push them further away.
Teachers must guard against taking the rejection personally, which can trigger subtle defensive resentment.
The fix is staying focused outward on the whole class and being consistently, unconditionally pleasant without pursuing the student.
Distrustful students come around over time when the teacher proves reliably trustworthy rather than trying to force a connection.
quotes: They seem happy around their classmates. They do their work. They follow directions.
But going to the student, approaching them and pushing for an explanation, is a mistake.
Unless you berated them, criticized them personally, or chided them with sarcasm, it isn’t about you. It’s about adults in general.
When you go to them with questions and conversation starters you make them uncomfortable and associate yourself with the fake charmers who disappointed them in the past.
It can make you want to get revenge. Not so much consciously, but as a defensive reflex. And you can’t hide resentment.
You only need to be consistently pleasant and in time even the most distrustful student will come around.
Have the courage to do what is right and best for your students long term, every day, and they’ll learn that it’s true.
